rewritten_text:
Many years ago, I became close friends with a man named William Legrand. He came from an old Huguenot family and had once been rich, but a series of disasters had left him poor. To escape the humiliation of his changed circumstances, he left New Orleans, where his ancestors had lived, and settled on Sullivan’s Island, near Charleston in South Carolina.

It is an unusual island, made almost entirely of sea sand. It is about three miles long and nowhere more than a quarter of a mile wide. A barely visible creek separates it from the mainland, creeping through a tangle of reeds and mud where marsh hens gather. As one might expect, the plants are sparse, or at least small. There are no large trees. The bristly palmetto does grow near the western end, where Fort Moultrie stands alongside some shabby wooden houses. In summer, these house people escaping Charleston’s dust and fever. Apart from this western tip and a strip of firm white beach facing the sea, the entire island is covered in thick sweet myrtle, a shrub much admired by English gardeners. Here it often reaches fifteen or twenty feet in height, forming almost impassable thickets and filling the air with its scent.

Deep within these thickets, near the island’s more distant eastern end, Legrand had built a little hut. He was living there when I first met him entirely by chance. Our acquaintance soon grew into friendship, for the solitary man had many qualities that interested me and earned my respect. He was well educated and unusually intelligent, but disliked humanity and passed through unpredictable moods of excitement and sadness. He owned many books, though he seldom read them. His main pleasures were shooting, fishing, and wandering along the beach or among the myrtles to look for shells and insects. His insect collection would have made even an expert like Swammerdamm envious. On these outings he was generally joined by an old Black man named Jupiter. Jupiter had been freed from slavery before the family lost its fortune, but neither threats nor promises could persuade him to leave young ‘Master Will,’ whom he considered it his right to follow and serve. It seems quite possible that Legrand’s relatives, believing his mind to be somewhat unsettled, had encouraged Jupiter’s stubbornness so that someone would watch over and protect their wandering kinsman.

Heavily armoured knights on heavily armoured horses could not make very rapid progress. These men would push along as quickly as possible, and with the roads now sound and clear of snow and mud, they could probably manage seven miles an hour. They would need fresh horses a couple of times and would get there around six, or shortly afterward. There would still be ample daylight. They would spot the white cloth I intended to fasten about my right arm, and I would assume command. We would ring the prison and release the king in next to no time. Considering everything, the affair would be sufficiently splendid and picturesque, although I should have chosen noon for its superior theatrical effect.

Then, to give myself another string to my bow, I decided to seek out some of the people I had recognized earlier and reveal who I was. That could extricate us without help from the knights. Caution was essential, however; the undertaking was dangerous. I needed magnificent clothes, and I could not simply dash into them all at once. I must advance by stages, purchasing one outfit after another in widely separated shops, each a little better than the last, until I reached velvet and silk and was equipped for my purpose. Off I went.

But that plan collapsed in a flash! At the very first corner I turned, I ran straight into one of our slaves, prowling about with a watchman. Just then I coughed, and he shot me a look that went clean through to my bones. I reckon he fancied he knew that cough. I stepped directly into a shop and moved down the counter, asking prices while keeping an eye on things sideways. The two had halted and were conferring as they peered through the doorway. I resolved to leave by the back, assuming there was a back exit. I asked the woman in the shop whether I might go out there to search for the runaway slave, supposedly concealed somewhere behind the premises. I explained that I was a disguised officer, that my partner was at the door guarding one of the murderers, and would she kindly tell him not to wait there? He should go immediately to the far end of the rear alley and stand ready to intercept the fugitive when I drove him out.

She was burning to see one of the murderers who had already become so famous, and set off at once to deliver my message.

As soon as Mrs. Musgrove found herself alone with Anne, she said, ‘Oh, Miss Anne, I do wish Mrs. Charles had some of your skill with those children. They behave like different creatures when you are with them! Usually, though, they are terribly spoiled. It is a pity you cannot teach your sister how to manage them. They are as fine and healthy as any children I have seen, poor little dears, and I say that without favouritism. But Mrs. Charles has no idea how to handle them! Goodness, they can be such a nuisance. I assure you, Miss Anne, it makes me less eager to have them at our house than I would otherwise be. I think Mrs. Charles is rather annoyed that I do not invite them more often. But you know how unpleasant it is to have children around when you must constantly tell them, “Don’t do this,” and “Don’t do that,” or can only keep them reasonably quiet by giving them more cake than they should have.’

Anne also heard this from Mary: ‘Mrs. Musgrove considers all her servants so reliable that questioning them would amount to treason. But I assure you, without exaggerating, her senior housemaid and laundry maid spend all day wandering about the village instead of working. I run into them wherever I go. I can scarcely visit my nursery twice without finding some sign of them. If Jemima were not the most trustworthy, dependable person alive, they would ruin her. She tells me they are always trying to persuade her to go walking with them.’ Mrs. Musgrove, meanwhile, had her own complaint: ‘I make it a rule never to interfere in my daughter-in-law’s affairs, because I know that would cause trouble. But I shall tell you, Miss Anne, since you may be able to put things right, that I think very poorly of Mrs. Charles’s nursery maid. I hear strange accounts of her; she is always out wandering. And I know myself that she dresses so extravagantly she could spoil any servant she meets. Mrs. Charles trusts her completely, I know. Still, I wanted to give you this warning so you could keep an eye on her. If you notice anything wrong, you need not hesitate to mention it.’

Mary also complained that when they dined with other families at the Great House, Mrs. Musgrove often failed to give her the place of honour her rank deserved. She saw no reason why being treated as one of the household should mean losing her proper place.
